Justice Kavanaugh authored a conceptually distinct dissent. He argued 
that “regardless of whether the Court is correct about the Duke Memorandum, 
the Nielsen Memorandum more fully explained the Department’s legal reasons 
for rescinding DACA, and clarified that even if DACA were lawful, the 
Depflrtm Ant would still rescind DACA for a variety of policy reasons. Unlike 
the majority, Justice Kavanaugh deemed the Nielsen memorandum itself a 
‘rule’ ” under the APA. The Nielsen memorandum, in Justice Kavanaugh’s 
view, “was akin to common forms of agency action that follow earlier agency 
action on the same subject.” And Justice Kavanaugh contended that 
precedents like State Farm required only “that courts assess agency action 
based on the official explanations of the agency decisionmakers, and not based 
on after-the-fact explanations advanced by agency lawyers during litigation (or 
by judges).” He conceded that cases like Overton Park “suggest that courts 
reviewing certain agency adjudications may in some circumstances decline to 
examine an after-the-fact agency explanation.” But that was because 
adjudications “imphcate the due process interests of the individual parties,” 
which required the “sUghtly more stringent restriction on post hoc 
explanations.” That reasoning did not apply to “an agency’s official explanation 
of an agency rule.” For its part, the majority responded to Justice Kavanaugh’s 
distinction between rulemaking and adjudication by observing that 
Kavanaugh “cite[d] no authority limiting [the] basic principle [of a 
contemporaneous explanation requirement]—^which the Court regularly 
articulates in the context of rulemakings—to adjudications.”
All told, DHS V. Regents was a significant, complex, and robust application 
of principles first articulated in cases like Chenery, Overton Park, State Farm, 
and Fox.
2. REVIEW OF FINDINGS OF FACT
Agencies regularly make factual determinations to support their 
decisions. These determinations include the specific and simple (e.g., the 
age of an individual seeking benefits) to the more general and complicated 
(e.g., the level of economic concentration in a particular industry). Agencies 
do so in the course of proceedings of varied formality—^from full-scale, 
formal adjudicatory proceedings on a record presided over by an 
Administrative Law Judge, to very informal determinations made in the 
course, for instance, of a routine enforcement proceeding. It is difficult to 
capture the variety in these determinations, or the judicial reaction to 
them, but this section will introduce some of the major questions with 
which courts have struggled.
